objectives: State the role of grids + whitespace.

slides.title: Typography fundamentals
slides.body:
Typography is the design of TEXT. Most UI is text; typography shapes most of the visual experience.

**Typeface vs font**:
- **Typeface**: family (Helvetica, Inter, Roboto).
- **Font**: a specific weight + style + size (Helvetica Bold 14pt).

**Classification**:
- **Serif**: small strokes at letter ends. Garamond, Times. Traditional, formal, used in print.
- **Sans-serif**: clean letterforms. Inter, Helvetica, Roboto, San Francisco. Default for screens; better readability at small sizes.
- **Slab serif**: heavy serifs. Roboto Slab, Lora.
- **Monospace**: fixed-width. Used for code (JetBrains Mono, Fira Code, Source Code Pro).
- **Display**: decorative, for headlines only.

**Anatomy** (typographer's terms):
- **x-height**: height of lowercase 'x'. Larger x-height = more readable at small sizes.
- **Ascender** / **descender**: parts above x-height / below baseline.
- **Counter**: enclosed space in letters (inside 'O', 'e').
- **Aperture**: the opening in letters like 'e', 'c'.

**Web fonts**:
- **System fonts**: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI'. Native to OS. Fast (no download). Used by default for performance + integration.
- **Custom fonts**: hosted via @font-face. Brand identity. Download cost (~50-300KB per family).
- **Variable fonts**: single file with multiple weights + widths. Flexibility without bloat.

**Web font formats**:
- WOFF2: modern standard, brotli-compressed.
- WOFF: older browsers fallback.
- TTF/OTF: original formats; large.

**Typographic scale**: ratio between sizes. Common: 1.25 (major third), 1.333 (perfect fourth), 1.5 (perfect fifth). Bigger ratios = more dramatic hierarchy; smaller = subtle. Material design uses 1.25; Apple uses dynamic type with custom scale per platform.

slides.title: Hierarchy, scale, + whitespace
slides.body:
**Visual hierarchy**: viewer's eye should be directed to the most-important element first.

Techniques to create hierarchy:
- **Size**: bigger = more important. H1 > H2 > body.
- **Weight**: bold > regular > light.
- **Contrast**: high-contrast (black on white) > low-contrast (gray on light gray).
- **Color**: bright/saturated > muted.
- **Position**: top-left receives attention first in LTR cultures (eye-tracking studies).
- **Spacing**: whitespace around an element draws attention.

Combine techniques but don't overdo. Two strong hierarchies competing = neither dominates.

**Type scale**: define ~5-7 type styles. Don't ad-hoc. Examples:
```
h1: 32px / bold / line-height 1.2
h2: 24px / semibold / 1.3
h3: 20px / semibold / 1.4
body: 16px / regular / 1.5
small: 14px / regular / 1.5
caption: 12px / regular / 1.4
```

**Line height** (leading): vertical space between lines. ~1.2 for headlines; ~1.5 for body. Too tight = hard to read; too loose = lines disconnect.

**Line length**: 50-75 characters per line for body. Too short = jerky eye movement; too long = lose place when wrapping. Use max-width.

**Whitespace** (negative space): essential, not wasted. Whitespace AROUND elements creates hierarchy + reduces cognitive load.
- Whitespace BETWEEN elements groups (small) or separates (large).
- Whitespace at PAGE EDGES (gutters) frames content.
- Whitespace within ELEMENTS (padding) makes them feel touchable + breathable.

**Grids**:
- 12-column grid (popularized by Bootstrap) is the web standard.
- Mobile-first: 4 columns mobile, 8 tablet, 12 desktop.
- Gutters between columns (16-32px).
- Margins at outer edges.

**Alignment**: align consistently (left, right, center, justified). Mixed alignment = chaos. Left-align for most LTR text; center for short callouts; right-align for numerical columns; avoid justification on screens (causes uneven word spacing).

slides.title: Color + accessibility
slides.body:
**Color in design**: signaling, emotional, hierarchical, branding.

**Color systems**:
- **HEX** (#FF0000): RGB in hexadecimal.
- **RGB**: red/green/blue, 0-255 each.
- **HSL** (hue/saturation/lightness): more intuitive for color picking. Hue is the rainbow position; saturation is intensity; lightness is brightness.
- **OKLCH** (perceptually uniform): newer, used in modern CSS color functions. Linear in perceived brightness + chroma.

**Color palette** for a product:
- **Primary**: brand-defining hue. Used for primary actions, brand expression.
- **Secondary**: supporting hue. Less prominent.
- **Semantic**: success (green), warning (orange/yellow), error (red), info (blue). Standard meanings.
- **Neutrals**: grays. 5-10 shades. Used for text, backgrounds, borders.

**Accessibility (WCAG)**:
- **Contrast ratio**: ratio between foreground + background. Minimum 4.5:1 for body text (WCAG AA); 7:1 for AAA. Larger text (18pt+) can be 3:1.
- **Color alone**: never use color as the ONLY indicator. Red 'error' should also have icon + text. 8% of men + 0.5% of women are color-blind.
- **Focus indicators**: keyboard users need to SEE which element has focus. Outline or border on :focus. Many designers remove this for aesthetics — never. WCAG 2.4.7.

**Color blindness types**:
- **Deuteranopia** (red-green, most common): trouble with red + green.
- **Protanopia**: similar; red appears darker.
- **Tritanopia** (blue-yellow): rare.
- **Achromatopsia** (no color): very rare.

**Tools**:
- **Color contrast checkers**: WebAIM, Stark plugin.
- **Simulators**: macOS accessibility settings show grayscale, color-blind modes. Useful for testing.
- **Palette tools**: Coolors, Paletton, Adobe Color, Tailwind palette.

**Dark mode**:
- Increasingly standard. iOS/Android system-wide setting.
- Inversion of background + text + tweaked semantic colors (errors stay red but more muted; borders less harsh).
- Tokens (next lesson) make dark mode 'just' a token-table swap.
- 30%+ of users prefer dark mode globally; higher in developer / power-user segments.

question.question: Check WCAG contrast
question.goal: Foreground: #767676 gray. Background: #FFFFFF white. WCAG ratio = ?

steps.prompt: WCAG contrast formula compares relative luminance: $(L_1 + 0.05)/(L_2 + 0.05)$ where L is luminance + L_1 > L_2. For #FFFFFF, L = 1.0. For #767676, L ≈ 0.18.
WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for body text. Does this pass?
steps.reveal: Just passes AA. Cutting it close — design-system gray should be slightly darker to provide margin. #757575 ≈ 4.6:1, safer.
No, fails AAA. For AAA compliance + comfort, use darker text. Many design systems aim for AAA in design tokens; degrade gracefully in some cases.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Contrast ratio} = (L_1 + 0.05)/(L_2 + 0.05); \geq 4.5 \text{ for AA, } \geq 7 \text{ for AAA}}$$ A core accessibility checkbox. Tools (Stark, WebAIM Contrast Checker, browser DevTools) check this automatically. Design tokens for the design system should pre-clear contrast for every text/background pair. Failing contrast is the #1 most-common accessibility violation in audits.

question.question: Your design uses RED text to indicate error + GREEN text for success. A user reports they can't tell the difference. Cause?
options: Most likely deuteranopia (red-green color-blindness; ~8% of men). Use color ALONG with icons + text labels, not color alone. Icons (× vs ✓), labels ('Error: ...' / 'Success: ...'), or distinct hue values (orange vs blue) help.
question.explanation: Color-blindness is common (especially red-green deuteranopia). Designing with color ALONE excludes ~8% of male users + ~0.5% of female users. WCAG 1.4.1 (Use of Color): color must NEVER be the sole means of conveying information. Best practice: pair color with icon + text. E.g., '× Error: invalid email' in red is fine because icon + text carry the message; red alone is not.

slides.workedSolution: Color blindness affects ~8% of men. WCAG 1.4.1: 'Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information.' Pair color with icons + labels. Simulators (macOS Accessibility, online tools) test for this. Many internal-tool designers think 'red = bad' is universal — common bug. Designs must work in grayscale + with color-blind simulation.

question.question: Type scale with ratio 1.25, base 16px. Size at the 4th step?
Implementing dark mode
question.prompt: Your app needs a dark-mode theme. Walk through what changes (colors, contrast, semantic intent) + what stays the same.
Explain in two or three sentences why typography choices are foundational to UI quality.
question.rubric: Mentions that the majority of UI is text; type choices (size, weight, line-height, font-family) determine reading ease, scanability, perceived hierarchy + brand. Good typography is the single biggest lever for making interfaces feel polished + readable; bad typography can sabotage even otherwise-good design.
